title: Babies receive everything
hook: in the East, infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion together

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iconostasis: a wall of faces that turns out to be a window. Your line was the icon screen.

The baby does not approve. She's been lowered into the warm water of the font three times, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and she's letting the whole church know about it. Then, still damp and wrapped in a towel, she's anointed with holy oil: forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, chest, hands, feet. And later, when the people come forward for communion, the priest lifts a small spoon to her mouth, a tiny portion of the consecrated wine. Baptized. Sealed with the Spirit. Fed at the altar. All before she can say a single word.
screen: `THREE TIMES INTO THE WATER.` → `ANOINTED WITH HOLY OIL.` → `A SPOON AT THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: First, the three. Catholics call baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist the sacraments of initiation: the way someone is brought all the way into the Church. The Catechism says plainly that in the Eastern rites, the initiation of infants begins with baptism, followed immediately by confirmation and the Eucharist. In the East, confirmation is called chrismation, and the priest anoints with the words: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Second, the West spreads them out. In the Latin Church, babies are baptized, and then come years of learning before first communion and confirmation later on. The Catechism holds the two side by side and ranks neither: the Eastern way shows the unity of the three sacraments; the Latin way, by keeping confirmation with the bishop, shows the bond with him. Same three gifts, different timing. Third, the reason the Catechism gives. When it describes the Eastern churches giving communion to the newly baptized, even little children, it recalls the Lord's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." Fourth, grace before understanding. A baby understands none of it. Doesn't know the creed, can't say amen, can't even hold her head up. That's the point both East and West make by baptizing infants at all: grace is a gift, not a prize. The East simply carries that logic all the way to the table.
screen: `BAPTISM, CHRISMATION, COMMUNION.` · `THE WEST SPREADS THEM OUT.` · `SUFFER THE LITTLE CHILDREN.` · `GRACE BEFORE UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `ALL THREE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a baby you know, or have held, or all the babies being carried to a font somewhere this week; then the tired parents, holding on, and the godparents who just promised something large. If you pray, pray the Our Father for them slowly, the prayer they'll learn one day. If you don't, simply wish them well: a long life, and people who keep their promises.
Babies receive everything. In the Eastern churches, infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion in one celebration. Today's word.
Your line: all three at once. Everything given, before anything is understood. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one, done.

howItsDone: In Eastern Catholic and Orthodox churches, an infant is baptized by triple immersion, chrismated with holy myron, and given communion from a spoon, usually in one celebration; Latin Catholics baptize infants and celebrate first communion and confirmation in later years.

chat.meaning: The Catechism says Eastern rites follow infant baptism immediately with confirmation and the Eucharist. Grace is a gift, not a prize.

chrismation.meaning: the Eastern name for confirmation, an anointing with holy oil

font.meaning: the basin of water used for baptism

creed.meaning: the Church's statement of what it believes

sacraments of initiation.meaning: baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist, which bring someone fully in

sources.quoted: Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 10:14 ('Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God'). CCC 1244 cites the line in a different wording; the script quotes the Douay-Rheims.

CCC 1233 paraphrased closely ('the initiation of infants begins with baptism, followed immediately by confirmation and the Eucharist'). CCC 1292 paraphrased for the two emphases; confirm the voice ranks neither.
Byzantine formula of chrismation ('the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit', CCC 1300) given without quotation marks.

Hook details (triple immersion; anointing of forehead, eyes, ears, mouth, chest, hands, feet; communion by spoon) follow common Byzantine practice; the anointed places vary slightly by church. Confirm.
'Grace is a gift, not a prize' summarizes CCC 1250 (infant baptism shows the pure gratuitousness of grace). Confirm.
Latin practice described generally ('years of learning, before first communion and confirmation later on'); order and ages vary by diocese, so no age is given.
